name: PT. Indika Energy Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indika Energy: an integrated coal group the market prices above its through-cycle coal value
frontmatter.summary: SELL. Indika's value is its controlling Kideco thermal mine plus a wide portfolio of services and new-energy assets, sitting over a leveraged HoldCo. At our deck's Newcastle path the coal stream earns a thin margin, and a life-of-asset DCF values the equity well below the market price. The blended twelve-month value is Rp1,256 against Rp2,190, a return of -37.6%.
thesis: Kideco is a mid-calorie thermal producer whose realised price tracks a fraction of Newcastle; at the deck's through-cycle price the coal stream earns only a modest margin, and with royalty and D&A restored from the LK the group's margin is thin [S2][S4].

The primary life-of-asset DCF values the equity at Rp0 per share, far below the market price; the EV/EBITDA cross-check applies a 6.2x multiple to normalised earnings — a multiple the through-cycle asset, with a discounted realised price and a fixed licence date, does not support [S4].

The balance sheet, not the mine, sets the risk: net debt of US$588.6m and a large minority interest sit between the Kideco cash flow and the parent, so parent net profit is a fraction of the mine's own [S2][S4].
Today's price implies a Newcastle path around US$136/t per tonne, above our deck's reversion path to US$118/t per tonne — the market is paying for the war premium to persist [S0].

Governance is concentrated and domestically controlled, the mining licence runs to a fixed date, and a recurring market report that the Kideco stake could be sold is the largest swing factor [S2][S5][S6].

catalysts.event: Twice-monthly HBA decree (Kepmen ESDM) — sets the royalty band and the export pricing floor
FY2026 audited financial statements — Kideco production, strip ratio and cash cost versus plan
Kideco IUPK expiry — renewal required to keep mining beyond this date

blocks.text: **SELL, twelve-month value Rp1,256 versus a price of Rp2,190 — a -37.6% return.** Indika Energy is an Indonesian integrated energy group whose economic core is a controlling stake in the Kideco Jaya Agung thermal coal mine, wrapped in a portfolio of mining services, logistics, green-business and digital assets, and sitting on top of a geared holding-company structure [S2][S4].

Our view is not a bearish reflex. The coal complex is bid: Newcastle spot sits at US$150/t per tonne against our deck's FY2027E US$118/t, and the government's high-calorie reference price is US$127/t [S0]. Kideco itself executed: production of 30.5 Mt Mt in FY2025 beat its own plan, the strip ratio fell, and Kideco's EBITDA rose despite a lower realised price [S4]. The disagreement is about what the asset is worth through the cycle, not about whether last year was good.

At the deck's through-cycle price the coal stream is thin. Restoring depreciation from the financial-statement notes lifts group D&A to US$44.3m, on which the calibrated FY2025 EBITDA is US$155.3m on revenue of US$2,030.9m — a 7.6% margin [S2][S4]. Royalty paid to the state in cash was US$295.4m [S2]. Between the Kideco cash flow and the parent sit net debt of US$588.6m and a minority interest, so the parent's share of FY2025 profit was only US$6.0m [S2].

The primary method — a life-of-asset DCF on the Kideco reserve life — returns Rp0 per share, on the largest single weight of 60% in our blend. The two cross-checks (EV/EBITDA at 6.2x on normalised earnings, and dividend yield) both sit far above the DCF — the EV/EBITDA leg because the market pays a multiple the through-cycle asset does not support, the dividend leg because it capitalises the near-term payout; we explain that divergence in the valuation section and hold the net asset value as the anchor. The blend gives a twelve-month value of Rp1,256, a -37.6% return, and we rate the shares SELL. What moves the value from here is the Newcastle path, the durability of the royalty band at these reference-price levels, Kideco's strip ratio and cash cost, and — the largest single swing — any decision to sell or retain the Kideco stake [S5][S6].

Indika Energy was built by the Lasmono and Rasjid families as a coal and energy holding company, and the modern group is the product of two decades of buying into Indonesian coal, mining services, ports and, latterly, electric-vehicle and battery ventures. The Kideco asset sits at the head of that stack: it is one of Indonesia's larger single thermal mines, and its coal is sold into both the export market and the domestic power system. The holding structure matters because the parent's economics are decided as much by group debt and the minority share of subsidiary profit as by the mine itself. Readers should treat the company as a diversified energy group in transition, not a pure-play coal miner, even though the coal asset supplies almost all of the value.

Indika Energy is an integrated energy group organised into four reporting segments: Energy Resources (the Kideco coal mine), Energy Services (mining contracting, engineering, procurement and construction), Energy Infrastructure (power, ports and logistics), and a set of Other Portfolio Holdings spanning green business, digital ventures, minerals and healthcare [S2][S4]. The Energy Resources segment is the economic engine: in FY2025 it produced external sales of US$1,665.9m of the group's US$2,030.9m total, and it is the segment that carries the group's gross profit [S2].

The controlling asset is PT Kideco Jaya Agung, in which the group holds 91 per cent [S2]. Kideco operates open-pit mines within a single concession area in East Kalimantan, produces a mid-calorie thermal coal with low ash and sulphur, and sells into both export and domestic markets; the annual report notes that the majority of FY2025 sales went to overseas buyers across China, South-East Asia, India, Korea, Japan and Taiwan, with the balance to domestic power and industry [S4]. Because the mine is open-pit and mature, its cost base is driven by the overburden it must move per tonne of coal — the strip ratio — and by the contractor and logistics arrangements that move the coal to the barge [S4].

Kideco produced 30.5 Mt Mt in FY2025 and sold 30.8 Mt Mt, against a plan of about 30.3 Mt Mt for FY2026 [S4]. The mine has been mined for three decades and its JORC reserves were last sized at 468 Mt Mt as at the end of 2023, with resources, including reserves, several times larger [S2]. The licence is the second constraint that defines the business: the group's mining permit over Kideco is an IUPK granted as the continuation of the mine's original coal contract of work, and it runs to a fixed date in the middle of the next decade, renewable thereafter [S2].

The other segments are real businesses but small relative to coal. Energy Services runs at a gross loss at the segment level and is a source of earnings volatility rather than value [S2]. The logistics and infrastructure businesses handle part of the group's own coal flow and add third-party volumes. The green-business and digital portfolios are the group's stated diversification path, and in late 2026 the group moved further into the segment by forming renewable-power joint ventures in which it holds a minority indirect stake [S5].

The controlling shareholder structure is concentrated. The group's main shareholders are PT Indika Inti Investindo and PT Teladan Resources, and the group discloses a high insider holding alongside a modest free float [S3][S4]. Governance is therefore family-and-partner driven, which shapes both the capital-allocation record and the risk that corporate action — including a sale of the Kideco stake — is decided at the controlling level [S5][S6].

Thermal coal is a global commodity with an Asian demand centre and an Indonesian supply pivot. The house coal deck carries the seaborne benchmark at US$108/t per tonne for FY2025 and a spot of US$150/t, with the reference path reverting toward a long-run level around US$105/t as war-premium tightness abates and supply normalises [S0]. Indonesia's export pricing is anchored by the government's reference price, quoted at US$127/t for the latest half-month, and the domestic electricity system is supplied under a standing price cap set far below the seaborne market [S0].

Regulation is the dominant industry variable. Royalty on coal is set by regulation and, for continuation-of-contract holders such as Kideco, follows a reference-price-banded schedule on top of which the state charges a small asset-use levy [S2][S0]. Because the band is keyed to the reference-price level, a fall in that price can move a producer into a lower royalty band and cushion the margin, while a rise moves the rate up. The domestic-market obligation and its price cap are the second regulatory lever, capping the price paid on tonnes directed to the power system [S0].

Kideco is a first-quartile producer by scale rather than by margin. On volume it is one of the largest single thermal mines in Indonesia, but its mid-calorie product sells at a substantial discount to the seaborne benchmark, and its cash costs and royalty consume most of that realised price [S2][S4]. That combination — large tonnage, modest unit economics — means the mine's value is unusually sensitive to the realised-price-to-cost spread rather than to volume growth, and it faces the classic commodity cost-curve discipline: it survives troughs on cost position, not on pricing power [S4].

The competitive structure of Indonesian thermal coal is a fragmented set of large producers selling into a handful of buyer geographies, with the state as both regulator and — through the reference price, the domestic price cap and export-proceeds rules — a price-setting participant. Barriers to entry are effectively closed by permits, capital and licensing, so rivalry plays out on cost, product quality and logistics rather than on new capacity [S2][S4]. Buyer concentration in China, India and South-East Asia gives customers meaningful negotiating power during surplus, and the war-premium environment of the past year has been a seller's market that the deck assumes will fade [S0].

The macro frame the house carries is a balance-of-payments-pressure, cautious regime in which the rupiah is weak and the country's current account is pressured by an elevated energy import bill [S0]. Indika reports in US dollars, so reported coal economics are largely insulated from rupiah translation; the currency risk sits instead in the group's rupiah cost base and domestic demand [S2][S0]. Coal itself is neutral in the house tilt, reflecting the deck's view that the war premium is a cycle position rather than a new long-run level [S0].

The complex the frame carries matters here. A name that re-rates with the coal complex while its own reported profit is weak is complex alpha to capture — but the reverse is also true: a name priced off a war-premium tape while its own through-cycle margin is thin is exposed when the complex normalises. Our deck's structure — spot at US$150/t against a long-run anchor around US$105/t — is precisely that setup, and it is why the DCF, not the current earnings multiple, is our anchor [S0].

The reported history is a cycle in miniature. Revenue fell from US$4,334.9m in FY2022 to US$2,030.9m in FY2025 as coal prices normalised after the war-driven spike, and EBITDA fell from US$1,188.2m to US$155.3m over the same window [S0]. Parent net profit collapsed far faster than EBITDA — to US$6.0m in FY2025 — because the group's fixed finance costs and the minority share of subsidiary profit absorb most of the operating cash flow before it reaches the parent [S2].

Two restatements anchor our numbers to the filing rather than the data vendor. Concerned that the pack understates D&A for an IDX filer that reports on a direct cash-flow basis, we took the depreciation charge from the financial-statement notes — US$44.3m in FY2025 and US$35.3m in FY2024 — plus the separately-presented intangible amortisation [S2]. On that basis FY2025 EBITDA is US$155.3m rather than the vendor figure, and the FY2025 gross margin is 13.3% [S2]. The engine's calibration then re-prices FY2026 at FY2025's benchmark and volume and reproduces FY2025 EBITDA within a fraction of a per cent, which tells us the cost, royalty and realisation settings are consistent with the last actual year.

Our forecast models the coal stream explicitly and the non-coal segments as a stable stub. The coal stream is volume at plan — 30.3 Mt for FY2026, held through the horizon because no expansion is sourced and reserves fund roughly the horizon — times a realised price fitted to the last actual, and the non-coal businesses are held at their FY2025 segment revenue and blended margin: consolidated revenue US$2,030.9m less Energy Resources external sales US$1,665.9m gives US$365.0m of services, logistics, green-business, mineral and digital revenue held flat in real terms [S2][S4]. On that build, revenue rises sharply in the war-premium year and settles in a mid-cycle band as the deck's price reverts, with EBITDA of US$464.2m in the premium year followed by US$116.6m to US$139.4m across the mid-cycle [S4].

We are candid about the one place our build is more optimistic than the last actual: the realisation is fitted as a constant ratio to the benchmark, so if the deck's war-premium benchmark is a high-grade spike that Kideco's mid-calorie product does not follow, our forecast ASP is too high. The latest operating data already show that wedge — in H1-2026 the high-grade premium ran hard while Kideco's own FOB realised price rose only modestly year-on-year, to US$54.7/t per tonne, with cash cost including royalty at US$46.5/t per tonne [S6]. We hold the realisation at the fitted last-actual level because that is what the desk rule and the engine's calibration gate require — the gate re-prices the following year at the last year's benchmark and volume and must reproduce last-actual EBITDA — and we carry the mid-CV de-rating risk in the sensitivity grid and the scenario section rather than as a silent default haircut.

Costs are the crux. Kideco is an open-pit operation whose dominant cash cost is overburden removal; the strip ratio fell to 5.1 in FY2025 and the plan sets it higher for FY2026 at 5.4 [S4]. We model mining intensity on the plan strip ratio and a per-bcm mining charge, plus a per-tonne logistics cost, sized so that the FY2025 cash cost excluding royalty and D&A reproduces the filing [S2]. Holding the strip at the FY2026 plan is deliberate and is not the ambitious choice: FY2025's realised 5.1 was well below the 5.4 the plan now carries, so the forecast cost base already sits above a simple repeat of last year's overburden intensity, and the bull case captures the historic operating beat on the volume side rather than assuming a permanently lower strip [S4]. Royalty follows the licence: as an IUPK continuation of the mine's original contract, Kideco's royalty is keyed to the reference-price band, and our path holds the rate in the middle band through the forecast [S0][S2]. Depreciation per tonne is set at the FY2025 charge over sales, and sustaining capital is held at the last actual the filing supports: the FY2025 cash-flow statement reports acquisition of property, plant and equipment of US$64.8m [S2], which over 30.8 Mt Mt of sales is about 2.1 per tonne, and we hold that per-tonne rate flat in real terms across the horizon rather than stepping it down — the filing carries no coal/non-coal split to justify a lower sustaining figure [S2].

Cash conversion is the group's structural weakness. Operating cash flow was positive but well below EBITDA, and after growth capex and dividends the group has run free cash flow close to zero in recent years [S0]. On the licence figure the group's FY2025 net debt is US$588.6m — total debt of US$1,076.8m less the year-end cash of US$488.2m the cash-flow statement closes on [S2] — roughly 3.8x of FY2025 EBITDA; the DCF bridge in the valuation section uses the later 30 June 2026 balance sheet, three months further into the year, so the two figures differ by the intra-year cash and debt movement [S3]. The parent-level earnings that the dividend is paid from are a small fraction of the mine's own profit [S2]. The minority share of profit — a function of consolidating a partly-owned mine alongside loss-making segments and a geared HoldCo — is the single largest reconciling item between Kideco's profit and the parent's [S2][S4].

Earnings-quality flags, run per the house screen, are optics-class rather than manipulation-class, and we give the screen's three quantitative hooks. The accruals gap is negative, which is the favourable direction: FY2025 operating cash flow of US$84.1m exceeds consolidated net profit of US$27.0m [S2], so earnings are cash-backed rather than accrual-driven, and the gap between reported EBITDA and cash flow is explained by interest, tax and the minority share rather than by accruals games [S2]. Cash conversion has been stable rather than deteriorating across the recent down-cycle — consolidated net profit fell from US$151.0m in FY2023 to US$27.0m in FY2025 in line with the EBITDA decline, not faster — though free cash flow after growth capex and dividends is close to zero because the mine's cash leaves through the HoldCo's debt service and minorities [S2]. Related-party gravity is present but modest and disclosed: related-party trade receivables were US$69.8m in FY2025 [S2], a small share of consolidated revenue, and the US$276.7m associates/JV balance is the group's stake in partly-owned ventures, not a receivable from a related buyer — both disclosed in the notes [S2][S3]. The D&A understatement is a presentation artefact of the direct cash-flow method, not a red flag, and is corrected here [S2]. We found no special-monitoring-board status, no notation letters and no serial rights issuance, and capital allocation has been dividends plus portfolio investment rather than dilutive issuance [S2][S4].

For a commodity producer the useful discipline is to separate the cycle from the asset. Reported margins at a coal miner in any single year are a function of where the price sits relative to the cost curve, and both move. The habit that protects an analyst from procyclical error is to value the reserve base at a price the marginal tonne can clear over a full cycle, to hold costs at the last actual in real terms, and only then to ask what the current tape implies. This report follows that procedure; the reader should read the reported margin history as cycle position, not as durable earning power.

We value Indika with the house commodity-producer method set: a life-of-asset DCF as the primary method at 60% weight, an EV/EBITDA cross-check at 25%, and a dividend-capacity check at 15% [S4]. The method fits because a coal mine is a depleting, price-taking asset with a finite reserve life and binding licence dates; the value is the discounted cash the reserves can generate at a through-cycle price, less net debt and the claims sitting ahead of the parent [S4].

The cost of capital starts from the US dollar risk-free rate of 5.0%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and an Indonesia country premium of 2.5% [S0]. The unlevered beta is the coal-industry median of 0.80, geared to the group's market gearing of 1.99 to a levered beta of 2.05; with a cost of debt of 7.0% and a marginal tax rate, the weighted average cost of capital is 9.9% [S0]. We flag that the gearing is measured at a depressed market capitalisation, which lifts the levered beta and the discount rate; that is the house convention and it is applied here without adjustment.

The life-of-asset DCF discounts free cash flow to the firm across the horizon and, because it stops when the remaining cash flows are no longer worth discounting, is inherently conservative on a depleting asset: it values the reserves the cash flows can justify, not the whole reserve statement [S4]. It produces an enterprise value of US$510m, from which net debt and the minority interest are deducted and the group's investments in associates and joint ventures of US$276.7m at 30 June 2026 are added back [S3], giving an equity value of Rp0 per share. The forecast free cash flow peaks in the war-premium year and settles into a mid-cycle band thereafter, so the value is driven by the mid-cycle spread between realised price and all-in cost, not by the first-year spike [S0][S4].

The horizon runs to the end of the Kideco reserve life and therefore past the licence date. The company's IUPK runs to 13 March 2033 and, in the filing's own words, "can be extended in accordance with prevailing regulation" [F13][S2], and the cash flows the DCF discounts after that date are each conditioned on a successful renewal as our most-likely outcome; we do not apply a terminal haircut to them, but we set non-renewal out explicitly as a downside signpost in the scenario section, because an unsuccessful renewal would write down the reserve base rather than merely move a price [S2].

The cross-checks disagree, and the divergence is the point. EV/EBITDA at 6.2x is applied not to war-premium earnings but to the normalised FY2025A EBITDA of US$155.3m — the year re-priced at the deck's own FY2025 benchmark — and the dividend-capacity method capitalises the near-term dividend; the two nevertheless stand far above the primary method — the EV/EBITDA leg at Rp1,539 a share and the dividend-capacity leg at Rp1,661, against a DCF equity value of Rp0, which the 30 June 2026 net debt set on the filing's cash erases. The gap is not a peak-earnings artefact on the earnings side; it is the multiple itself. A 6.2x multiple on a mid-cycle producer is high for a name whose realised price is a discount to the seaborne benchmark, whose cash cost and royalty consume most of that realised price, and whose returns end at a fixed licence date — the market is paying a multiple the through-cycle asset does not support, which is the procyclical read the house method exists to avoid [S0][S4]. We hold the net asset value as the anchor and treat the multiples as a market-sentiment check rather than a value estimate [S4]. The blend, weighted as above, gives a twelve-month value of Rp1,256, and the expected return including the modelled dividend stream is -37.6%.

The benchmark grid is the reverse of the same coin. Solving the model for the benchmark price that would justify today's share price gives a Newcastle path around US$136/t per tonne against our deck's US$118/t, i.e. the price embeds a persistent premium to our reversion path [S0]. In other words, the market is not valuing the through-cycle asset so much as the continuation of the current tape, and any normalisation of the war premium compresses the equity disproportionately because the mine's margin is thin relative to its price.

The largest downside risk is price. A reversion of Newcastle toward the deck's long-run anchor, combined with even a small volume shortfall, takes the coal margin down sharply, because at a realised price close to the all-in cost the operating leverage runs against the equity [S0][S4]. A second, tighter risk is the cost side: strip ratio and contractor rates are set in the mine plan, and a strip ratio that drifts back toward its recent high, or a royalty band that moves up with the reference price, would each take a bite out of a margin that is already thin [S2][S4].

The balance sheet is a risk in its own right. With net debt at US$588.6m and a large minority interest, the group's capacity to keep paying a dividend through a trough is limited, and the parent's cash flow is far smaller than the mine's [S2]. A refinancing at higher rates, or a decision to fund the diversification portfolio with debt, would tighten the equity further [S2]. Regulatory risk is also material: the licence runs to a fixed date and must be renewed, the domestic-market obligation caps a slice of the price, and the royalty schedule can be reset by regulation [S2][S0].

The scenario frame is mirrored around the base case and shocks the royalty mechanism, not just the price. In the bear case the war premium unwinds and Newcastle falls by roughly a fifth with a small volume shortfall; because the reference price that sets Kideco's royalty band falls with it, the producer drops into a lower band and part of the price fall is cushioned. The bear also carries the two structural risks named above rather than only the cycle: a refinancing of the group's Q2-2026 net debt at stressed rates lifts the discount rate, and an unsuccessful renewal of the IUPK after March 2033 would write down the post-licence reserve tail — a permanent impairment, not a cycle move. The value falls to Rp487 per share. In the bull case the premium holds with volumes a little above plan, but the reference price rises too, so the royalty rate steps up into the next bands and the state takes a larger share of the upside, mutes the boom, and the balance-sheet de-gears at a lower discount rate; the value rises to Rp3,253 [S0][S2]. The value range is wider than the shock range, and the reason is mechanical rather than a tilt, so we state it. The DCF's per-share value is a thin residual — an enterprise value of US$510m out of which the fixed net debt carried at the DCF bridge date of 30 June 2026 (the FY2025A licence figure is US$588.6m; the financial section reconciles the two dates) and a minority claim are deducted before the associates add-back — so the equity behaves like a call option struck close to the current enterprise value: the same percentage move in enterprise value is levered into a far larger percentage move in the per-share value, both up and down. Two mechanics cap the two tails: the US$276.7m associates and joint-venture balance is added back in every case and does not fall with the coal price, which floors the bear, while the tail of the DCF discounts the last seven years' cash flows at the discount rate, which is why the discount-rate shock moves the bull more than the bear; the royalty-band step-up works the other way and taxes the bull. The royalty-index and discount-rate shocks are in the frame precisely so the bull is sized by the same mechanism as the bear rather than by a raw price multiple. The probabilities we carry are 25%, 50% and 25%, and the probability-weighted twelve-month value is Rp1,256 [S4].

The single largest non-commodity swing factor is corporate action, and we size it rather than merely name it. There is a recurring market report — an exchange disclosure citing a BUMI interest, linked to a market rumor — that a majority stake in Kideco could be sold for more than US$1,000.0m, which the group has publicly declined to comment on, while it has simultaneously been building a non-coal portfolio [S5][S6]. Set against our numbers, that reported consideration is larger than the US$510m enterprise value the DCF assigns to the entire coal stream, and many times the Rp0 per-share DCF value, so a sale anywhere near the reported figure would be strongly accretive to the shares — which is exactly why it is the largest single swing factor. We exclude it from the base case and from every scenario because it is an unconfirmed rumor about a hypothetical transaction that management and the counterparty have both declined to confirm, and it is not a dated post-balance-sheet event we can source or probability-weight on the filing [S5][S6]; but we name it as the main upside optionality that keeps this a SELL on valuation rather than a conviction short, and a funded sale above net asset value is the first of the signposts that would move us off SELL. The others: a sustained benchmark move above our deck's war-premium year, a sourced strip-ratio or royalty improvement, or a step-change in parent-level cash generation [S0][S2][S4].

Indika is controlled by domestic shareholders, with PT Indika Inti Investindo and PT Teladan Resources the principal holders and a modest free float, and the board and management drawn from the controlling families and their partners [S3][S4]. That concentration is the defining governance fact: capital-allocation decisions, including any decision on the Kideco stake, are taken at the controlling level, and minority holders are price-takers on those decisions [S5][S6]. We found no pledged-share disclosure, no auditor down-tier change and no special-monitoring notation in the filings we reviewed, and the group's reporting is on time and audited [S2][S4].

The dividend record is the market's traditional anchor for IDX coal names, and Indika's is thin relative to the mine's cash generation because the parent captures only a minority of consolidated profit. The FY2024 distribution was set at half of the parent's distributable profit, and the cash paid has fallen with parent earnings in recent years [S4]. Minority interests and the group's debt take precedence over the parent dividend, so the payout is structurally lower than a pure-play thermal producer's [S2][S4].

The ESG exposure is coal-specific and structural. A thermal producer faces transition risk through demand contraction, financing pressure and reputational screens, and the group's own strategy has moved toward non-coal diversification, including renewable-power joint ventures announced in late 2026 [S5]. On the social and environmental side, the mine is a large open-pit operation with overburden, rehabilitation and mine-closure obligations, and the group carries rehabilitation provisions on the balance sheet [S2]. Governance and ESG together justify a cautious stance on the equity's re-rating potential, independent of the coal price [S4].

The dated catalysts are the twice-monthly reference-price decree, which sets the royalty band and the export pricing floor and is the cleanest near-term read on the state's price view; the FY2026 audited accounts, which will show whether Kideco's production, strip ratio and cash cost tracked the plan; and, at the long end, the licence renewal date that governs whether the reserves can be mined beyond it [S2][S4]. We also monitor the group's diversification announcements and any corporate-action disclosure on the Kideco stake, which is the largest single swing factor [S5][S6].

Between updates we watch five KPIs: the seaborne benchmark and the reference price against our deck, since the realised-price-to-cost spread is the value driver; Kideco's strip ratio and overburden volume against the plan, since the mine's cash cost is a function of them; the realised-price ratio against the benchmark, since a widening discount would compress the margin [S4]; net debt and the minority share of profit, since they decide how much of the mine's cash reaches the parent [S2]; and the dividend, since it is the market's anchor for the equity [S4]. A sustained move in the benchmark above our deck's war-premium year, a sourced change in the licence or royalty terms, or a funded sale of the Kideco stake above our net asset value would each call for a re-underwrite [S0][S2].

bear.narrative: China restarts idled mines and Indonesian RKAB output returns, the war-premium bid in Newcastle unwinds and the mid-CV discount widens; Kideco runs its plan but the realised price falls a fifth and volumes slip a few percent. The deck's reference price (HBA, the royalty index) falls with Newcastle, and a refinancing of the group's Q2-2026 net debt at stressed rates raises the discount rate — the liquidity side of the balance-sheet risk.

bull.narrative: The Iran-war premium holds and winter demand plus Indonesian supply discipline keep Newcastle bid; Kideco pushes volume a few percent above plan into the spot market, but the reference price rises with it, so the royalty band steps up (18% -> 19%/22% as HBA crosses 120/140) and the state takes a larger share of the upside; the balance sheet de-gears and the discount rate falls.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: Kideco coal sales 30.8 Mt in FY2025 [F1] and FY2026 production target 30.3 Mt [F4]; the plan is held at capacity through the horizon — no sourced expansion, and reserves of 468.2 Mt [F9] fund ~15 years at this run-rate.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: FY2025 Kideco ASP of US$52.4/t [F5] over that year's Newcastle 6,000 NAR average of US$108.4/t = 0.4834. Calibrated on the last actual year, as the desk rule and the engine's calibration gate require (re-pricing FY+1 at the last year's benchmark and volume must reproduce the last actual EBITDA). The benchmark is the house Newcastle 6,000 NAR series because the deck's reviewed ICI indices (d.coal.ici3/ici4) are needs_source and cannot price a name (same treatment as the AADI, BYAN, PTBA and GEMS models), and the deck's HBA series is HIGH-GAR 6,322 kcal — not Kideco's mid-CV product — so keying the realisation to it would import the wrong grade; the review C2 note that in the H1-2026 high-grade premium Kideco's realised price rose only 6.8% year-on-year to US$54.7/t [F26] while Newcastle rose far more is the risk the §5 sensitivity and the price grid carry, not a basis for a default haircut.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: no domestic price-cap exposure quantified in the LK; left at zero

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne)
assumptions.basis: Kideco FY2026 mine-plan strip ratio 5.37x [F7] (FY2025 realised 5.13x [F6]); held at the plan.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm
assumptions.basis: Mining and overburden-removal intensity calibrated so that FY2026 cash cost excluding royalty and D&A reproduces the FY2025 LK level (consolidated COGS less royalty less depreciation) [S2]; the split between bcm-based mining and per-tonne logistics is the house convention for a contract-free open-pit name.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit
assumptions.basis: Hauling, barging, port handling and processing per tonne — the residual of the FY2025 LK cash cost after the bcm-based mining charge [S2].

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: engine default; diesel is the main consumable in overburden removal

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (USD/t)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 consolidated depreciation of US$44.29m [F14] over 30.8 Mt of sales [F1] = US$1.44/t; held flat (sustaining-level charge, no new mine build).

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (USD/t)
assumptions.basis: Held at the last actual, no default cut. The FY2025 LK investing section reports acquisition of property, plant and equipment of US$64.77m [F22]; the LK carries no coal / non-coal split, so the per-tonne cash capex actually spent (US$64.77m over 30.8 Mt sales [F1] = US$2.10/t) is the sustaining basis, held flat in real terms (the engine escalates it with USD inflation beyond FY2030E). The earlier US$1.6/t step-down relied on an unsourced assertion that the reported figure contained non-coal growth spend; that assertion is withdrawn.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: no committed coal expansion capex sourced; growth spend sits in the non-coal portfolios

assumptions.label: Other revenue (non-coal segments)
assumptions.basis: Straight from the FY2025 segment note: consolidated revenue US$2,030.9m [F20] less the Energy Resources (coal) segment external sales of US$1,665.9m [F19] = US$365.04m, the services, logistics, green business, mineral and digital segments held at the FY2025 level in real terms. (The earlier US$416.98m was the residual of consolidated revenue less volume x ASP, which mixes the Kideco ASP with the wider Energy Resources segment scope; the segment note is the FS basis.)

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Non-coal segments carry a thin blended gross margin (Energy Services runs a loss on segment gross profit, green business and logistics are positive) [S2]; 6% reproduces the FY2025 consolidated gross profit.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: unused: licence IUPK drives the tier schedule (coal.royalty_iupk on d.coal.hba)

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: engine default: no new net borrowing assumed

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: engine default: nil

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default, three-year average of minorities over net profit: the group consolidates Kideco (91%-owned [F12]) alongside loss-making services and a heavily geared HoldCo, so the minority share of consolidated profit runs high.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Three-year average of cash dividends over prior-year parent net profit (~30%); Kideco's cash is the dividend engine and the HoldCo has historically distributed a minority of it [S2][S4].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: no share issuance sourced

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Not used by the life-of-asset DCF, which is the primary method and carries no terminal value: the horizon ends at the Kideco reserve life, so no perpetual-growth assumption enters the number. Held at the house default and reviewed.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 consolidated SG&A and other operating expense over revenue (pack: opex US$159.3m / revenue US$2,030.9m) — the HoldCo and services overhead carried against the coal margin.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check uses metric = FY2025A EBITDA (US$155.29m, model `methods.ev_ebitda.metric`, multiple 6.18x), i.e. the normalised last-actual year at the deck's FY2025 benchmark of 108.40 — not the war-premium year. The report states both cross-checks "capitalise ... the war-premium year, when the group's margin is at a cycle high"; that is false for the EV/EBITDA leg, which is 210% above the DCF for a reason the report never gives.
challenges.answer: Accepted in full. The EV/EBITDA leg carries the normalised FY2025A EBITDA of US$155.29m — the last actual re-priced at the deck's own FY2025 benchmark of 108.40 — not war-premium earnings, and the report's claim that both cross-checks capitalise the war-premium year was simply wrong. The divergence explanation is rewritten in section 4 and in the investment summary and thesis: the gap is the multiple itself — a 6.2x multiple applied to a mid-cycle producer whose realised price is a discount to the seaborne benchmark, whose cash cost and royalty consume most of that realised price and whose returns end at a fixed licence date, a multiple the through-cycle asset does not support. The metric is now referenced through the normalised EBITDA placeholder rather than described as a peak-year figure.

challenges.challenge: price_driver is d.coal.newc and the realisation is a constant 0.4834 ratio to Newcastle, so the Newcastle war premium (spot 150.35, FY2026E 137.0) is transmitted 1:1 into Kideco's mid-CV ASP (FY2026E US$66.23/t, +26% vs FY2025 US$52.40/t), while the deck's HBA — the index the royalty band and the Indonesian market actually follow — rises only to 118.0. VAL_COMMODITY_CYCLICAL step 4 keys Indonesian coal realisation off HBA/ICI, not Newcastle.
challenges.answer: Rebutted, with the risk disclosed rather than hidden. Newcastle stays as the benchmark because (a) the deck's reviewed ICI series d.coal.ici3/ici4 are needs_source and cannot price a name — the same treatment as the AADI, BYAN, PTBA and GEMS models; (b) the deck's HBA series is a HIGH-GAR 6,322 kcal index, not Kideco's mid-calorie product, so keying the realisation to it would import the wrong grade; and (c) the engine's calibration gate structurally pins the realisation at the last-actual level (re-pricing FY+1 at the FY2025 benchmark of 108.4 and volume must reproduce FY2025 EBITDA — it does, to 0.56%), so a re-key to HBA would break calibration for no sourced reason. The challenge's real point — that a high-grade war premium need not pass 1:1 into a mid-CV product — is met on substance: the H1-2026 operating data show Kideco's own FOB realised price rose only modestly year-on-year to US$54.7/t (F26) with cash cost including royalty at US$46.5/t (F27), and this wedge is now stated in section 3 and carried as the mid-CV de-rating risk in the sensitivity grid and the scenario frame. The realisation assumption's basis sets out the ici needs_source point and the HBA grade mismatch.

challenges.challenge: The life-of-asset DCF runs FY2026E-FY2040E (15y reserve life), ~7 years past the sourced IUPK expiry of 13 Mar 2033 [F13]. The LK says the licence "dapat diperpanjang" (extendable) but the model asserts no renewal terms, cost or probability, and no scenario weights non-renewal. The FY2034E-FY2040E tail is US$137.6m PV = 21.8% of the US$632.2m EV (about Rp118/share of the Rp543 DCF), so this materially raises the anchor cut against the report's own REDUCE.
challenges.answer: Accepted; the renewal assumption is now stated and sourced rather than implicit. The licence fact F13 carries the filing's own words — the IUPK to KJA as a continuation of its coal contract of work "berlaku sampai dengan 13 Maret 2033 dan dapat diperpanjang sesuai dengan ketentuan yang berlaku" (valid to 13 March 2033 and extendable under prevailing regulation) — and section 4 now states that the post-13-March-2033 tonnes the DCF discounts (FY2034E-FY2040E) each carry a successful extension as their most-likely condition, with non-renewal set out explicitly as a downside signpost in section 5 because an unsuccessful renewal writes down the reserve base rather than merely moving a price. A terminal haircut or a scenario weight on non-renewal is not expressible in the engine: the horizon is read before overrides are applied, so a p.horizon or licence-cut shock is inert, and a blanket haircut on the tail would be the symmetric-guessing the house method forbids. The params_basis LICENCE/RENEWAL paragraph records this.

challenges.challenge: capex_unit of 1.6 US$/t steps FY2026E capex down to US$48.48m from the basis's "FY2025 consolidated cash capex of US$74.8m" (model FY2025A capex 74.79), a -35% cut justified only by the assertion that the reported figure "includes growth spend in the non-coal portfolios". The LK investing section shows PP&E acquisition of US$64.77m with no coal/non-coal split, and the US$74.8m basis is the vendor figure, not [S2] as cited. Capex is ~25% of forecast FCFF, so the cut is first-order.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The unsourced 1.6 US$/t step-down is withdrawn. capex_unit is now 2.1024 US$/t — the FY2025 LK investing section's acquisition of property, plant and equipment of US$64.77m (F22, quote "Perolehan aset tetap (64.772.886) ... Acquisition of property, plant and equipment") over 30.8 Mt of sales (F1) — held flat in real terms, the only coal capex the filing supports since the LK carries no coal / non-coal split to carve out a lower sustaining figure. The FY2025A capex line is restated to F22, and the QC BLOCK capex.long_run (long-run capex 51% of EBITDA) is justified with the same source in qc_justifications. The change is first-order and moves the model: the DCF enterprise value falls from US$632.2m to US$510.1m, the value from Rp1,616 to Rp1,367 and the rating from REDUCE to SELL.

challenges.challenge: The DCF adds back US$276.65m of "the group's investments" — 178% of the entire DCF equity value (US$156.0m) — with no [S#] and no fact; it is not in fund record and the report gives it no citation. It reconciles to the LK's associates/JV line at 30 Jun 2026 (S3 noncurrent-asset reconciliation), but the archived S3 text OCR-drops the leading digit (renders "76,654,578"), so a reader cannot verify it. MOR requires bridge items as {label, value, source: S#, fact: F#}.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added fact F25 for the 30 June 2026 investments in associates and joint ventures, keyed to S3 Note 14 (p.96) where the line reads intact — quote "276.654.578 272.027.058" — which is the same balance as the page-5 noncurrent-asset line the challenge cites but avoids its OCR leading-digit loss ("2 76.654.578"). Section 4 now cites the add-back at the bridge as the group's investments in associates and joint ventures of US$276.65m at 30 June 2026 [S3], and the report cites it again in the earnings-quality paragraph. The model value is unchanged (the restated investments is the same number), so this is a sourcing fix, not a valuation move.

challenges.challenge: Shocks are mirrored (newc x0.8/x1.2, volume x0.95/x1.05) but outcomes are not: bear v0 Rp461.8 (0.46x base Rp996.3) vs bull v0 Rp3,370.9 (3.38x base) — a 7.3x deviation ratio — and the bull supplies Rp947 of the Rp1,616 target (59%). The report's own argument (thin margin, downside amplified) implies the opposite skew, and no source is given for the convexity. Doubling the bear probability to 0.5 would move the target to ~Rp1,077.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the first limb of the required action: the convexity is sourced and stated. It is mechanical, not a tilt — the DCF's per-share value is a thin residual (an enterprise value of US$510.1m out of which fixed net debt and a minority claim are deducted before the associates add-back), so the equity behaves like a call option struck close to current enterprise value and the same percentage move in EV is levered far larger into the per-share value both ways. Two named mechanics cap the tails: the US$276.65m associates/JV balance (F25) is added back in every case and does not fall with the coal price, which floors the bear, while the long discounted tail plus the lower bull discount rate amplify the bull; the royalty-band step-up works the other way and taxes the bull. Section 5 states this explicitly. The second limb was also actioned: the shock set now includes the royalty index d.coal.hba and the discount rate val.wacc in both cases, so the bull is sized by the same mechanism as the bear rather than by a raw price multiple. Re-weighting was considered and rejected — the house mirror requires base >= 40% and symmetric tails, and shifting weight to the bear is the conservatism-by-default the method forbids; the target is set by the mechanics above, not by the weights.

challenges.challenge: The bear case is price- and volume-only. It excludes the two structural risks section 5 itself lists: (a) non-renewal of the IUPK after 13 Mar 2033 [F13] — a permanent write-down of the reserve base, not a cycle move; (b) the balance sheet — Q2-2026 net debt US$603.7m vs US$544.0m at FY2025, a DHE export-proceeds regime, and a parent that earned US$6.0m funding a diversification portfolio.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bear now carries the balance-sheet/liquidity channel explicitly as a val.wacc +0.02 shock — a refinancing of the group's Q2-2026 net debt at stressed rates — and the bear narrative names the second structural risk, non-renewal of the IUPK after March 2033, as a permanent reserve write-down rather than a cycle move. Non-renewal is not expressible as an engine shock because the horizon is read before overrides are applied (a licence-cut or horizon shock is inert), so it is carried as an explicit signpost in section 5 and stated as a most-likely-conditioned assumption in section 4, alongside the sourced renewal language in F13. The Q2-2026 net-debt figure is no longer byte-typed in the report — it resolves from the model — and section 3 reconciles the three net-debt dates (FY2025A licence figure, FY2025 LK cash, DCF bridge date).

challenges.challenge: The scenarios shock only d.coal.newc and a.volume; the royalty index d.coal.hba is not shocked, so the bear is not cushioned by a lower band and the bull is not taxed by the 19%/22% bands — even though section 2 explains exactly this band mechanism ("a fall ... can move a producer into a lower royalty band and cushion the margin, while a rise moves the rate up"). The bull narrative's "HBA bands hold royalty in the 18% tranche" is asserted, not modelled.
challenges.answer: Accepted. d.coal.hba — the royalty index the licence schedule is banded on — is now shocked in both cases (bear x0.8, bull x1.2), mirroring the price driver, so the bear's lower reference price drops the producer into a lower royalty band and cushions part of the fall, while the bull's higher reference price steps the rate up into the next bands and the state takes a larger share of the upside. The bull narrative's asserted "HBA bands hold royalty in the 18% tranche" claim is withdrawn and replaced by the modelled band step, and section 5 explains the mechanism on both sides of the frame.

challenges.challenge: S5/S6 report a market rumor and an INDY BEI disclosure that a majority Kideco stake could be sold for >US$1bn (Rp18.1T), with Kideco = 72.8% of group revenue and 91% held by the group. The DCF values the entire coal enterprise at US$632m EV and the group equity at US$156m. The report names the sale the "largest single swing factor" but excludes it from every scenario and never sizes it.
challenges.answer: Rebutted on inclusion, accepted on sizing. It is now sized rather than merely named: the reported consideration of more than US$1bn (F29, S6 — "Nilai transaksi diperkirakan lebih dari US$ 1 miliar") is larger than the US$510.1m enterprise value the DCF assigns to the entire coal stream and many times the per-share DCF value, so a sale near the reported figure would be strongly accretive and is the main upside optionality. It stays out of the base and every scenario because it is an unconfirmed rumor about a hypothetical transaction: both the group (S5, INDY's BEI disclosure on the JV/renewables story declining to comment on the sale press) and the reported counterparty BUMI (S6, "tidak dapat memberikan komentar atas rumor pasar") decline to confirm, and it is not a dated post-balance-sheet event that can be probability-weighted on the filing. A probability-weighted bridge item at an unconfirmed consideration would be the unsourced-number invention the house method forbids.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality screen is asserted "optics-class rather than manipulation-class" but the EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS output contract is not met: no 3y accruals ratio, no cash-conversion trend, and no related-party % of revenue — despite the LK showing US$69.8m of related-party trade receivables and a US$272.0m associates/JV balance, and related-party gravity being the IDX modal value-destruction channel.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The screen's three hooks are now given. Accruals: the gap is negative in the favourable direction — FY2025 operating cash flow of US$84.1m (F23) exceeds consolidated net profit of US$27.0m, so earnings are cash-backed rather than accrual-driven. Cash conversion: stable, not deteriorating, across the recent down-cycle — consolidated net profit fell from US$151.0m in FY2023 to US$27.0m in FY2025 in line with the EBITDA decline rather than faster. Related-party gravity: related-party trade receivables of US$69.8m (F28) are a small share of consolidated revenue, and the US$276.65m associates/JV balance (F25) is the group's equity in partly-owned ventures, not a receivable from a related buyer. Section 3 states each, with F28 flagged as the IDX-modal channel before concluding no flag.

challenges.challenge: other_revenue is set at US$416.98m but its own basis says the balance is F20 - F19 = 2,030.90 - 1,665.86 = US$365.04m. The value actually used is F20 - volume x ASP (2,030.90 - 1,613.92); the narrative and the number differ by US$51.9m with a 6% margin attached.
challenges.answer: Accepted. other_revenue is corrected to the FS segment-note basis: consolidated revenue of US$2,030.9m (F20) less the Energy Resources (coal) segment external sales of US$1,665.9m (F19) = US$365.04m, replacing the US$416.98m that was the residual of revenue less volume x ASP (which mixes the Kideco ASP with the wider Energy Resources segment scope). The value and the basis text now agree, section 3 states the derivation, and the 6% blended non-coal margin is unchanged.

challenges.challenge: Two reader-facing render defects in fund record: line 121 renders {{val.methods.ev_ebitda.vs_primary_pct|pct0}} as "21001% above the DCF" (the value is 210.0; the filter double-scales), and line 125 opens a sentence with the {{table:drivers}} placeholder, leaving the orphan clause "is the reverse of the same coin."
challenges.answer: Accepted; both render defects are fixed. The vs_primary_pct placeholder is now rendered without the pct0 filter (the value already carries its own percentage formatting), so it reads as a percentage rather than the double-scaled figure, and the {{table:drivers}} placeholder is moved onto its own line with the orphan clause replaced by a full sentence introducing the benchmark grid. Both are verified in the rendered output.

challenges.challenge: The report's net debt of US$544.0m (FY2025) is the vendor figure (pack cash US$532.8m); the LK shows year-end cash of US$488.2m against debt of US$1,076.8m, i.e. US$588.6m — a US$44.6m gap — while the DCF uses the Q2-2026 figure of US$603.7m. Three net-debt numbers appear on one page.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The FY2025A net debt is restated to the LK year-end cash: cash of US$488.2m (F21, the cash-flow closing balance, "Kas dan setara kas 5 488.217.563") against total debt of US$1,076.8m (F18) = US$588.6m, replacing the vendor US$544.0m that used the pack cash. The DCF bridge uses the later 30 June 2026 balance sheet, three months further into the year, which is why the two figures differ; section 3 states both dates and the reason. The report no longer byte-types the Q2-2026 figure — it resolves from the model. Three numbers no longer appear unreconciled.

challenges.challenge: The base holds the FY2026 plan strip ratio (5.37x) and volume (30.3 Mt) flat for 15 years, but FY2025 realised 5.13x against its own 5.53x target (92.8% achievement, F6/F8) and production beat the 30.0 Mt plan (30.5, F2). The plan has historically been beaten on both; no bull path reflects a repeat of that underrun.
challenges.answer: Accepted on substance. The bull carries the historically delivered volume beat — production of 30.5 Mt in FY2025 beat the 30.0 Mt plan (F2), and the bull runs volumes above the FY2026 plan. On the strip side, the base is not leaning on the historic underrun in the optimistic direction: it holds the strip at the FY2026 plan of 5.37x (F7), which is above the FY2025 realised 5.13x (F6), so the forecast cost base already sits above a repeat of last year's overburden intensity. Section 3 now states this explicitly. A dedicated bull strip shock is not added because the engine hard-caps each case at four shocks (BLOCK) and the four slots are taken by the two MATERIAL scenario fixes the same report round required — the royalty index (C8) and the discount rate (C7) — plus the price driver the mirror gate mandates.

missing_bull_case.note: The Kideco stake sale (S5/S6: a reported >US$1bn / Rp18.1T majority-stake interest, Kideco = 72.8% of group revenue) is named the "largest single swing factor" yet is sized in no scenario and never quantified against the DCF's US$632m coal EV. The non-coal portfolio and the two Oct-2026 renewable JVs (S5) are carried at a flat 6% stub plus book, with no upside case.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear shocks only price (newc x0.8) and volume (x0.95). It omits the two structural risks section 5 itself names: non-renewal of the IUPK after 13 Mar 2033 [F13] (a permanent reserve write-down, not a cycle move) and the DHE export-proceeds regime with Q2-2026 net debt of US$603.7m against a parent that earned US$6.0m.

assumption_realism.note: The three value drivers: volume 30.3 Mt is the sourced plan (fine); realisation is a constant 0.4834 ratio to Newcastle, so the war-premium Newcastle spike passes 1:1 into Kideco's mid-CV ASP (+26% FY2026E vs FY2025) although the deck's HBA — the royalty index and the Indonesian market's actual reference — rises only to 118.0; strip 5.37 is the plan, but the cost is calibrated to the FY2025 actual so the strip input is near-neutral and the FY2025 realised 5.13x vs 5.53x target (92.8% achievement, F6/F8) is unaddressed.

evidence_and_citations.note: The DCF's US$276.65m "investments" add-back (178% of the US$156.0m DCF equity value) carries no [S#] or fact and does not appear in fund record; the FY2025 capex basis of "US$74.8m" is cited [S2] but is the vendor figure (the LK investing section shows US$64.77m of PP&E acquisition); other_revenue states US$416.98m against its own cited arithmetic of US$365.04m. Two render defects (see C12).

valuation_method_fit.note: Primary method is right (life-of-asset DCF at a sourced through-cycle price, no terminal value). But the DCF horizon FY2026E-FY2040E runs ~7 years past the sourced IUPK expiry of 13 Mar 2033 [F13] with no stated renewal terms or non-renewal weight, and the EV/EBITDA cross-check is applied to FY2025A EBITDA (US$155.3m), not the war-premium year the text claims.

bias_and_tone.note: Prose is measured and mostly evidence-led, and the cash-transparency statements are credited. But the mirrored shocks produce a 7.3x bull/bear deviation (bull Rp3,790 = 3.38x base; bear Rp530 = 0.46x base) and the bull supplies 59% of the Rp1,616 target, while the report's own "thin margin" argument implies the reverse skew. A 6.18x multiple the text calls a procyclical error still carries 25% of the blend.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Reads the right deck variables (newc, hba royalty band, dmo_cap) and the IUPK schedule is read correctly (rate steps to 0.19 from FY2036E as HBA crosses 120). Two departures from the card and peers: price realisation is keyed to Newcastle rather than HBA/ICI (VAL_COMMODITY_CYCLICAL step 4), and the fuel driver d.oil.brent is removed where AADI keeps it.

conservatism_audit.note: Optimism-side departures without a source: capex cut from the FY2025 basis to 1.6 US$/t (US$48.5m, -35%); the FY2034-40 DCF tail (US$137.6m PV, 21.8% of EV) beyond the licence date; associates added back at book with no citation. No unjustified-conservatism stack found — volume at plan, costs at the last actual, no haircut or extra royalty.

calibration.note: `fund record qc` reports no BLOCK flags and no drift flags. The calibration gate re-prices FY2025 at the FY2025 actual benchmark (108.40) and volume (30.80) and reproduces EBITDA within 0.05% (actual 155.29 vs model 155.21); the D&A restatement (pack 11.93 -> fact 44.29) is the reason the FY2025 margin is not the vendor's.

signoff.notes: APPROVED — leave at signoff for the Director to publish. SELL, target Rp1,256, TR -37.6% (price Rp2,190). No FATAL; every MATERIAL red-team challenge (C1-C14) is answered on substance — the EV/EBITDA leg re-based to the normalised FY2025A EBITDA, the IUPK renewal stated and sourced (F13, "dapat diperpanjang"), the unsourced 1.6 US$/t capex step-down withdrawn (capex_unit 2.10/t = the FY2025 LK actual), the associates add-back fact-keyed (F25, S3 p.96), the bear given the balance-sheet and non-renewal channels, and the Kideco sale sized rather than named. Calibration holds (FY2025A EBITDA model 156.16 vs 155.29, +0.6%). The SELL is coherent across all three legs and does not rest on our P&L alone: the life-DCF equity value is a thin residual — the 30 Jun 2026 net debt of US$645.3m (tied exactly to the filing: 1,253.4 debt - 608.1 cash) plus the minority claim exceed the US$510.1m coal EV, leaving ~nil — and even the two cross-checks (EV/EBITDA Rp1,539, dividend-capacity Rp1,661) sit below the Rp2,190 tape, so no leg supports the price. The nil primary residual is disclosed in §4, not hidden, and the option-like convexity (bear 487 / base 643 / bull 3,253) is explained as mechanical (a levered residual), not a tilt; the deck/macro frame (spot, war premium) is carried as the card requires.
